group.label: Personalisation (beta)
group.comment: Tailors what shoppers see to what they have bought, searched for and chosen. Three controls; the machinery behind them lives under Advanced. Tracking is always on — profiles are built and events recorded whether or not personalisation is applied, so the moment you switch it on it is warm, and an A/B test starts with weeks of labelled history rather than from zero. Personalisation re-orders results; it never hides a product. The Personalisation Dashboard (FastMagento menu) shows what all of this is doing.

field.label: Apply To Storefront
field.comment: Use profiles to re-order category listings, search results, up-sells and cross-sells. Off by default. With this off, profiles are still built and can be inspected via bin/magento fastmagento:profile:inspect.

field.label: Personalisation Weight
field.comment: How hard personalisation pushes, in one dial. Normal is the tuned default. Less halves it — for stores where merchandising must dominate. More nearly doubles it. Auto hands the dial to the store itself: a nightly job compares the conversion of personalised shoppers against the A/B control and nudges the weight toward whatever converts best — so Auto needs the A/B test running, and holds still (saying why, on the dashboard) until it has enough data to act on.

field.label: A/B Test
field.comment: Splits shoppers 50/50: half get personalisation, half get the storefront exactly as it is today. The dashboard compares what each half buys — this is the only way to know personalisation is selling more, rather than merely ranking differently. Assignment is sticky (the same shopper stays in the same half across visits and login) and costs the page cache nothing. Required for Auto weight.

group.label: Advanced
group.comment: The machinery under the three dials above. The defaults are the measured ones; change these when you know why.

field.label: Build Shopper Profiles
field.comment: Aggregate purchase, review and category history into per-shopper profiles. Runs off the request path and does not affect the storefront on its own. Leave on: turning it off means a cold start whenever you enable serving.

field.label: Record Searches And Facet Selections
field.comment: The two strongest signals a storefront already sees and normally throws away. A purchase says what someone ended up with after stock, price and delivery had their say; a search or a facet click says what they were actually looking for. Recorded at the moment it happens and costs no SQL. On a store with a full-page cache the browser reports facet selections, because a cached listing page never reaches PHP at all — so keep the storefront JavaScript deployed, and bin/magento fastmagento:doctor will tell you if it is stale. Independent of the other two switches — you can record without profiling, and profile without serving.

field.label: Impact — Category Listings (0-100)
field.comment: How hard personalisation pushes on a PLP. Lower than the others by default: a category page has a merchant-chosen order and personalisation should nudge it, not overrule it. 0 disables it for this surface.

field.label: Impact — Search Results (0-100)
field.comment: Applied after textual relevance, so a shopper searching for something specific still gets it. 0 disables it for this surface.

field.label: Impact — Related, Up-sell & Cross-sell (0-100)
field.comment: Highest by default: a recommendation row exists to be relevant to this shopper, and the merchant's link set is still the only pool it can draw from. 0 disables it for this surface.

field.label: Preselect The Variant A Shopper Prefers
field.comment: On a configurable product, open on the size and colour this shopper usually buys, when they are in stock. Every other option stays selectable and a link they followed with its own choice still wins. This is the one place a size preference is worth acting on: catalogue-wide it is too common to re-order a listing, but among one product's variants it is exactly the right signal.

field.label: Maximum Boosted Values Per Surface
field.comment: This is a cache setting before it is a relevance one. A personalised page needs its own full-page-cache entry, and the number of entries is the number of distinct boost combinations your shoppers produce — so raising this multiplies cached variants of every page. 2 is a deliberate default: the second-strongest value in a real affinity already carries a small fraction of the first's weight, so a third rarely changes an order. Raise it only if personalisation feels too blunt, and watch your cache hit rate when you do.

field.label: Stated Requirements — Attribute Mapping
field.comment: Where a shopper tells you what they need in the search box, this is what turns it into ranking. Format shape:attribute_code, comma separated — e.g. year:model_year,dimension:bed_size, mapping a recognised shape (a four-digit year, a dimensional spec) to whichever attribute holds that data on your catalogue. Somebody searching "sheets for a queen bed" or "filters for a 2021 model" has told you the single most useful thing about themselves on their first visit, before they have bought anything; on most stores that lands in a text box and is thrown away. Leave empty and nothing happens: the requirement is still recorded, it just does not rank. A requirement re-orders like everything else — the products that fit come first, the rest stay on the page.

field.label: Strength Of A Stated Requirement (%)
field.comment: How hard a requirement the shopper stated ranks against a preference we inferred. 100 = the same as the strongest preference; the default of 300 puts it decisively ahead, which is the intended order — what someone typed beats what we worked out about them. Scaled down by how sure we are they meant it, so a requirement guessed from one search ranks far below one they have repeated.

field.label: Exploration Slot (% Of Page One)
field.comment: Every popularity-driven ranking is a rich-get-richer loop: what ranks gets seen, what gets seen gets bought, what gets bought ranks. Your newest stock never enters the loop. This reserves the last slots of page one for products that have not been shown enough to judge — measured, on this store the five most-shown products had ~490 impressions and zero sales while the best converter had been shown 69 times. At 10, roughly one card in ten is a product the shopper would not otherwise have seen; it still matched their search. The least-shown fitting product gets the slot, and rotates out automatically once it has been seen enough to judge. 0 turns it off. Shopper-chosen sorts (price, name) are never touched.

field.label: Weight Of Searches And Facets vs Purchases (%)
field.comment: 100 = a search or facet click counts the same as a purchase. The default of 150 counts it half again as much, because a purchase records what someone settled for once stock, price and delivery had their say, while a search records what they asked for before any of that interfered. Set to 0 to profile from purchases only.

field.label: Minimum Affinity Concentration (0-100)
field.comment: How consistently a shopper must pick the same value before it is used. A shopper who buys every colour we sell has no colour preference, and boosting one would invent it. Lower this only if personalisation feels too timid.

field.label: Minimum Confidence (0-100)
field.comment: How much history is needed before a preference counts. Guards against treating a single purchase as a lifelong taste.

field.label: Recency Half-Life (days)
field.comment: How quickly older purchases stop counting. At 180, a purchase from six months ago carries half the weight of one from today. 0 disables decay entirely.
